---
title: "Week 2 demo: carbonate response to acid"
---

Why can two waters at pH 7.50 respond so differently to the same acid dose?

Use with [carbonate species and alkalinity](../carbonate-gases/lec.qmd), the [reference sheet](../carbonate-gases/reference.qmd), and [exercise 2](../carbonate-gases/exercise.qmd#same-ph-different-acid-response). This working week groups aquatic composition, carbonate, and organic matter.

## Predict first

Compare 1.00 and 0.100 mmol/L total inorganic carbon at the same initial pH. Predict which water has the larger pH decrease when 0.050 meq/L strong acid is added.

## Questions to try

1. Choose **Water A: more carbon**, then **Water B: less carbon**. Record initial alkalinity, final alkalinity, and final pH. Relate the difference to the initial inventory rather than to a different starting pH.
2. Choose **No acid added**, then move only the fixed carbon total. At the same pH, what changes: fractions, concentrations, or alkalinity?
3. Choose **Check pH 8.35 fractions**. Check the bicarbonate fraction against the hand calculation in the carbonate exercise.
4. Return to Water B and increase the acid dose. Watch the final-state marker and explain the redistribution toward CO₂*. Negative alkalinity is possible; it is not a negative concentration.

## Hand check and static reference

| Closed-water case | Initial carbon | Initial alkalinity | Acid added | Final model pH |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Water A | 1.00 mmol/L | 0.9356 meq/L | 0.050 meq/L | 7.235 |
| Water B | 0.100 mmol/L | 0.09382 meq/L | 0.050 meq/L | 6.252 |

At fixed total carbon, final alkalinity equals initial alkalinity minus acid dose.
The final pH satisfies that alkalinity balance and the carbonate species balance.
At prescribed pH 8.35, species fractions are approximately 0.009799 CO₂*,
0.979939 HCO₃⁻, and 0.010261 CO₃²⁻.

## Model conditions

Use dilute freshwater at 25 °C, pK₁ = 6.35, pK₂ = 10.33, and Kw = 10⁻¹⁴ (the water ion product). Activities are approximated by concentrations. Each acid addition conserves the selected dissolved inorganic-carbon total; gas exchange, minerals, biological change, other buffers, and dilution are excluded. The distribution curves show fractions at prescribed pH; the final marker additionally satisfies the changed alkalinity balance. The internal numerical solution is a calculation aid, not a new student programming task.

## Explain the result

Explain why moving along a species curve is insufficient to simulate a specified acid addition unless the carbon and alkalinity constraints are also applied.
